extracted.intended_audience: humanities scholars, faculty, academic administrators, librarians, and others interested in developing humane evaluation metrics for humanities research and teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Reflective guidance on designing and implementing humane, process-oriented metrics for humanities research and teaching that avoid perverse incentives and remain contestable and context-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from 'excellence' to standards of quality, credibility, and soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace vague, comparative appeals to 'excellence' with concrete standards of quality, credibility, and soundness when evaluating work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post summarizes Neylon et al.'s critique: 'excellence' lacks content, concentrates resources, produces homogeneity, and encourages gaming (e.g., citation cartels). Quality/credibility/soundness allow reviewers to judge thoroughness, appropriateness, and the integrity of the process rather than flashiness or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the research process (process-oriented evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift the evaluation focus to the research or teaching process rather than solely on outputs or the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process measures ask whether work was thorough, complete, and appropriate. Soundness emphasizes the methods and steps taken. Example indicators include whether feedback was sought and incorporated or whether replication-relevant steps were taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indicators of process as suggestive evidence (indicators may not be proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat observable steps in the process as indicators that the final product may be better, while acknowledging that indicators are suggestive rather than definitive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that evidence certain steps were taken (e.g., broad citation, seeking feedback) could suggest higher-quality outputs, but contested interpretations are possible; indicators should be used as part of assessment, not as conclusive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple indicators rather than relying on a single metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow for several complementary indicators to capture different dimensions of value instead of reducing assessment to one metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple indicators reduce the risk of overfitting behavior to a single measure ('you get what you measure'). The author suggests using varied signals (e.g., citations, student engagement, feedback practices) to form a fuller picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany quantitative indicators with narrative interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Require those being evaluated (e.g., faculty) to communicate indicators and provide a narrative explaining possible meanings and limitations of those indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative analyses help contextualize metrics (e.g., why students took another course may signal enthusiasm or other factors like grading). This preserves faculty judgment and offers richer evidence for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design metrics to minimize perverse incentives and gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and guard against the tendency of metrics to shape behavior in undesirable ways ('you get what you measure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of gaming include citation cartels and incentivizing easier grading to attract students. Metric design should consider likely manipulations and aim to reduce incentives that distort practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep values contestable and open to negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the set of values and evaluative criteria remain subject to ongoing contestation and renegotiation rather than being sedimented into unquestioned rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post warns that when values become fixed they can exclude or silence groups. Regular re-evaluation prevents ossification and helps surface who might be excluded by current norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncritical use of personal characteristics as evaluative values
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about including personal traits (e.g., kindness, compassion) as formal evaluative criteria because they can be weaponized to silence dissenting or oppressed voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop participants argued that demands for certain personal behaviors can suppress necessary criticism. If such traits are used, include safeguards to prevent misuse against marginalized voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage broad citation practices as an indicator of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use breadth of citation as a potential indicator that scholarship considered multiple perspectives and counter-arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing broadly may strengthen scholarship by forcing authors to consider disagreement. However, broad citation is an indicator not proof, and citation metrics themselves are vulnerable to manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and evaluate evidence of feedback-seeking and incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether authors sought feedback during the process and meaningfully incorporated it into their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that feedback was sought and integrated can be a process indicator suggesting thoroughness. Reviewers should consider how feedback influenced revisions rather than merely its existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain and respect faculty judgment in interpreting metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve the role of disciplinary and faculty judgment as central to assessing what indicators signify about quality and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that faculty narrative and judgment are appropriate complements to metrics; relying solely on metrics risks reproducing existing orthodoxies and power structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'blue sky thinking' and good-faith principles in metric development processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt practices for deliberation that encourage imaginative, aspirational thinking (blue sky) while committing to good-faith engagement among participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop methods included blue-sky brainstorming and rules to assume colleagues speak in good faith; these practices helped surface values without being derailed by immediate practical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and promote institutional practices that enable contestation and negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop indicators that capture whether institutional processes facilitate ongoing contestation and negotiation of values (rather than entrenchment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post links good scholarly outcomes to processes that encourage disputation and revision; metrics could track presence of deliberative mechanisms, revision cycles, or forums for negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider scale and transferability when implementing metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether proposed metrics and processes can scale across different communities, institution types, and contexts and how funders or powerful actors affect adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions include scalability to multiple academic communities and how to change culture when powerful people/institutions benefit from the status quo. The author notes funders (e.g., Mellon) can influence accrediting agencies and presses.
